Instructions to candidates: Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively (at least ONE question from each section). Each question carries 25 marks.

Candidates are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of material.

questions.enonce_markdown:
"Though their views were different, their main focus was on the universe." Discuss this assertion with reference to the Milesian cosmologists.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Milesian school takes its name from Miletus, an Ionian city on the coast of Asia Minor, where in the 6th century BC Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes began to ask what the world is made of and how it came to be, and to answer without appealing to the will of the gods as Homer and Hesiod had done. Western philosophy is traditionally said to begin with them. The assertion says that their views differed but that their main concern was the universe. The problem is whether the unity of their question outweighs the diversity of their answers, and whether the universe was really their only concern.

**Thesis: the universe was their common and main focus.**
(i) *The search for the arche.* Aristotle reports that the first thinkers looked for the arche, the first principle or primary stuff from which all things come, in which they consist and into which they return. Each Milesian gave his own candidate, but each was asking about the origin and the make-up of the whole cosmos.
(ii) *Thales* held that the primary stuff is water; the earth, he thought, rests on water, and Aristotle reports his saying that all things are full of gods, meaning that nature is alive and moves of itself.
(iii) *Anaximander* chose the *apeiron*, the boundless or indefinite, which has no beginning, is not any one of the known elements, and from which the opposites (hot and cold, wet and dry) separate out to form the worlds. He described the earth as hanging freely at the centre, held in place by equilibrium, because it has no reason to move in one direction rather than another. His surviving saying that things pay penalty to one another for their injustice according to the order of time shows that he saw the universe as ruled by a law of balance.
(iv) *Anaximenes* chose air; by condensation and rarefaction air becomes wind, cloud, water, earth and stone, or fire. He thus gave the first mechanism to explain how one stuff becomes many things.
(v) *What they share.* All three are cosmologists: they explain the origin and structure of the world, they use natural causes and not myth (naturalism), they reduce the variety of things to one underlying reality (monism), and they assume that the world is orderly and intelligible. On this point the assertion is sound.

**Antithesis: their views differed, and the universe was not their only concern.**
(i) *Differences of doctrine.* Water, the boundless and air are different answers. Anaximander is understood by later commentators to have gone beyond Thales: a determinate stuff such as water is itself one of the opposites and could not produce its opposite, so the first principle must be indeterminate. Anaximenes returned to a definite stuff, but gave it a mechanism.
(ii) *Differences of method.* Thales reasoned from observation (the moisture in seeds and nourishment); Anaximander reasoned by abstraction and by the principle of balance; Anaximenes reasoned by a quantitative change of density. The three men did not repeat one another: the school developed through criticism, a teacher-pupil tradition in which each corrected the other. This shows that the main interest was less a fixed doctrine than a way of enquiring.
(iii) *Concerns beyond the universe.* Thales is counted among the Seven Sages and tradition credits him with practical wisdom, with geometry and with astronomy, and Aristotle reports that he ascribed soul to the magnet. Anaximander is credited with a map of the world and a model of the heavens, and his saying on justice mixes moral and cosmic language. So their enquiry touched the knowledge of nature, the soul and justice as well as the universe.
(iv) *A limit of the evidence.* We know the Milesians only from fragments and from reports by Aristotle and later writers, who read them in their own categories (the arche as material cause). The claim that the universe was their main focus may partly be a reading back.

**Synthesis.** The difference lies in the answers, not in the question. Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes shared one problem, the origin and order of the cosmos, and solved it in three ways. The assertion is therefore broadly correct, with one qualification: by asking for a rational explanation of the universe the Milesians founded a critical way of thinking that went beyond cosmology to knowledge, the soul and justice.

**Conclusion.** The Milesian cosmologists disagreed about what the first principle is, but they agreed that the universe is to be explained by reason and by natural causes. Their main focus was indeed the universe, yet their importance lies as much in the method they started as in the answers they gave.
